exhibits.title: Control of Fire

site.label: Gesher Benot Ya'aqov and Qesem Cave

regions.note: Older claims (c. 1.5 million years) at Koobi Fora and Chesowanja are contested.

exhibits.change: Humans kept fire alive — warmth, light, protection and cooked food on demand.
exhibits.context: The earliest secure traces are burned bone and plant ash inside Wonderwerk Cave about a million years ago. By around 400,000 years ago repeated hearths appear at sites such as Qesem Cave in Israel and Beeches Pit in England. Whether early humans could reliably start fire, or only captured and kept it, is harder to tell from the record.
exhibits.significance: Fire extended the day into the night, made new foods digestible, drove off predators, and later became the tool for hardening wood, treating stone, firing clay and smelting metal — the root of almost every later energy technology.

uncertainty.note: When fire moved from occasional use to habitual control is actively debated; burned material can also come from natural fires.

exhibits.title: Ash in Wonderwerk Cave
exhibits.change: Microscopic ash and burned bone, deep inside a cave where wildfire could not reach.
exhibits.context: Micromorphology published in 2012 showed burned bone and ashed plant remains in an Acheulean layer about 30 metres inside the cave, suggesting fire was used in place rather than blown in.
exhibits.significance: One of the strongest early cases for fire used by humans.

exhibits.title: Hearths by the Jordan
exhibits.change: Burned flint clusters at the same spots, layer after layer, point to repeated fires.
exhibits.context: At this lakeside site, burned flint microartifacts cluster in patches that look like hearths, recurring across many occupations. Later analysis suggested fish there were cooked.
exhibits.significance: Evidence that fire was being used habitually outside Africa far earlier than once thought.

exhibits.title: Cooking

when.display: direct evidence from c. 780,000 years ago

exhibits.change: Heat did part of the digestion, releasing more energy from the same food.
exhibits.context: Tooth enamel changes in fish remains from Gesher Benot Ya'aqov suggest cooking at controlled, moderate temperatures. Some researchers argue cooking began much earlier, with Homo erectus, based on the reduction in tooth and gut size.
exhibits.significance: Cooked food is softer, safer and more energy-dense — a possible driver of larger brains and smaller teeth.

uncertainty.note: The 'cooking hypothesis' timing (c. 1.8 million years ago) is not supported by direct archaeological evidence.

sources.note: Zohar et al. 2022, Nature Ecology & Evolution.

exhibits.title: Homo heidelbergensis
exhibits.change: Large-brained humans in Africa and Europe, near the root of both Neanderthals and our own species.
exhibits.context: The name is used for Middle Pleistocene fossils such as the Mauer jaw in Germany and the Kabwe skull in Zambia. These humans hunted large animals and made handaxes and, later, prepared-core tools.
exhibits.significance: Often placed close to the last common ancestor of Neanderthals and modern humans.

uncertainty.note: Many researchers consider the category a catch-all; its membership and even its name are disputed.

exhibits.title: Hafted Points
exhibits.change: A stone point bound to a wooden shaft — the first composite tool.
exhibits.context: Damage and resin-like traces on points from Kathu Pan 1 have been read as evidence of hafting onto spears around half a million years ago. Joining parts of different materials requires planning several steps ahead.
exhibits.significance: Composite tools — separate parts combined into one working whole — are the ancestors of nearly every machine.

uncertainty.note: The dating and the hafting interpretation have been questioned.

exhibits.title: The Oldest Wooden Structure
exhibits.change: Two logs joined by a cut notch — woodworking for building, not just tools.
exhibits.context: Waterlogged sediments at Kalambo Falls preserved two interlocking logs, one notched to hold the other, dated by luminescence and reported in 2023. They may be the base of a platform or walkway.
exhibits.significance: Wood almost never survives this long; the find hints at a lost world of early construction.

uncertainty.note: A single find; its purpose is uncertain.

exhibits.title: Prepared Cores

regions.note: Argued to be a local development, c. 325,000 years ago.

exhibits.change: Toolmakers shaped a core first, so the next blow released a flake of a chosen size and shape.
exhibits.context: The Levallois technique requires shaping a stone in advance to predetermine the flake it will yield. It appears in Africa and Eurasia in the later Middle Pleistocene and may have arisen more than once.
exhibits.significance: A step toward standardised, efficient production — many uniform blanks from one prepared block.

uncertainty.note: Whether it spread from one origin or was reinvented in several regions is debated.

exhibits.title: Neanderthals

site.label: Sima de los Huesos, Atapuerca (early lineage)

exhibits.change: Another kind of human, adapted to Ice Age Eurasia, with its own culture.
exhibits.context: Neanderthals made sophisticated stone tools, controlled fire, hunted large game, used pigments and produced birch-tar adhesive. They disappear from the record around 40,000 years ago, but their DNA survives in most living people.
exhibits.significance: They show that complex behaviour was not unique to Homo sapiens.

uncertainty.note: Neanderthal symbolic behaviour and the causes of their disappearance remain debated.

exhibits.title: Obsidian from Afar
exhibits.change: Toolstone moved 25–95 km — the first hint of networks between groups.
exhibits.context: Middle Stone Age layers at Olorgesailie contain obsidian from distant sources and pigment-processing tools, appearing during a period of environmental instability (reported 2018).
exhibits.significance: Long-distance movement of materials suggests contact or exchange between groups — the distant roots of trade.

exhibits.title: The Schöningen Spears
exhibits.change: Balanced wooden throwing spears, found beside the horses they hunted.
exhibits.context: Found in a coal mine in the 1990s, the spruce and pine spears are over two metres long and shaped like modern javelins. They lay among butchered horse bones on an ancient lakeshore.
exhibits.significance: Clear evidence of planned big-game hunting with purpose-made weapons.

uncertainty.note: The site's age has been revised; estimates range from about 300,000 to about 200,000 years.
